questiontext.text: What underlying structure best describes a binary heap?

answer.text: A complete binary tree, usually stored in an array

feedback.text: Correct — the completeness lets it pack contiguously into an array.

answer.text: A binary search tree kept in sorted order

feedback.text: No — a heap only orders parent vs child, not left vs right.

answer.text: A linked list of nodes with parent pointers

feedback.text: No — the standard implementation is an array, not a linked list.
No — that is a different, more complex structure.

generalfeedback.text: A binary heap is a complete binary tree satisfying the heap property, and completeness makes an array representation natural and pointer-free.

questiontext.text: In a min binary heap of n elements, what is the time complexity of extract-min?

feedback.text: Correct — after removing the root you sift down along one root-to-leaf path.
That is find-min; removing it requires restoring the heap.
No — sift-down touches only one path of height log n.
No — that is the cost of extracting all n elements.

generalfeedback.text: Extract-min moves the last element to the root and sifts it down one path of height O(log n).

questiontext.text: Using a 1-based array, the parent of the node at index i is stored at which index?

feedback.text: Correct — children are at 2i and 2i+1, so the parent is at floor(i/2).
No — 2i is a child index, not the parent.
No — that is not how the implicit tree maps to the array.
No — that off-by-one applies to 0-based indexing, not 1-based.

generalfeedback.text: In a 1-based array the parent of i is floor(i/2) and the children of i are 2i and 2i+1.

questiontext.text: Building a heap from an unordered array of n elements via bottom-up heapify runs in:

feedback.text: Correct — a tighter analysis over node heights sums to linear time.
That is the loose bound; the tight bound for bottom-up build is O(n).
No — you must process every element.
No — heapify is far cheaper than that.

generalfeedback.text: Most nodes are near the bottom with tiny sift-down cost; summing height*count telescopes to O(n).

questiontext.text: In a min binary heap, finding the minimum element takes O(1) time.

feedback.text: Correct — the minimum is always at the root (array index 1).
The minimum is always the root, so it is O(1).

questiontext.text: An in-order traversal of a binary heap visits the elements in sorted order.

feedback.text: No — a heap only constrains parent vs child, not left vs right siblings.
Correct — heaps are not sorted like a BST; only the min/max is at the root.

questiontext.text: In a 1-based array heap, the left child of the node at index i is stored at index ______ (answer as an expression in i).

feedback.text: Correct.
Correct.
Correct.

questiontext.text: Which statements about a binary min-heap are true? (select all that apply)

answer.text: Insert runs in O(log n) via sift-up

feedback.text: Yes — a new leaf bubbles up at most one path height.

answer.text: It is the standard array-based priority-queue implementation

feedback.text: Yes — heaps back most priority queues.

answer.text: The array representation needs child pointers per node

feedback.text: No — indices are computed arithmetically, no pointers stored.

answer.text: Every left subtree holds smaller keys than every right subtree

feedback.text: No — that is a BST property; heaps do not order siblings.

generalfeedback.text: Binary heaps give O(log n) insert/extract and O(1) find-min, store no pointers, and back most priority queues; they are not search-ordered like a BST.
